title: Your RAG Found the Right Document. So Why Is the Answer Still Wrong?
excerpt: I read 106 wrong answers where retrieval worked. Half came from old and new versions of the same page, a fifth from the right document arriving without the right passage.
content:
I read 106 wrong answers where retrieval worked. Half came from old and new versions of the same page, a fifth from the right document arriving without the right passage.

You built retrieval, measured it, and it works: the right document comes back almost every time. The answers are still wrong often enough that nobody trusts them.

In my system the right document reached the model for 99 to 100% of questions on every setup I tried, yet about one answer in five was wrong. So I went through every wrong answer where the right document had been retrieved, 106 of them, and labelled why each failed, with AI assistance.

Only 2 of the 106 were the model reasoning badly from good evidence. Most went wrong before it wrote a word: the documents disagreed with each other, or the passage holding the answer never arrived. The best fix wasn’t a better model or better search. Telling the system which document was current lifted accuracy from 85% to 93%.

The setup

This comes out of a larger project, written up in [I Tested 10 Ways to Stop an AI Chatbot From Lying. The Fix Wasn’t the AI.](https://medium.com/@sandeshjung/i-tested-10-ways-to-stop-an-ai-chatbot-from-lying-the-fix-wasnt-the-ai-2479f0ce0f65?sharedUserId=sandeshjung). In brief:

Found the document, missed the passage

Most retrieval metrics ask whether the right document came back. But a model doesn’t read documents. It reads the handful of passages you cut from them, six in my case. So for each of the 82 answerable questions I copied out the exact sentences an answer needs, then checked whether they were among the passages the model was shown.

Hybrid search, a re-ranker and every safety feature after them left passage recall stuck at about three in four. Only changing what went into the context moved it.

And whether the passage arrived decided whether the answer was right:

When the passage is missing, the model rarely makes something up. It answers from the nearest passage it does have, from the right document, with a citation. That is why these answers look trustworthy, and why document-level recall hides them.

Cause 1: two versions of the truth

53 of the 106 wrong answers, from 12 questions. The archived 2025 pages are near-duplicates of the current ones, so they retrieve just as well. A superseded passage reached the model on 39 of the 82 answerable questions, on every setup until I started dropping them. Nothing inside a passage says which version is in force.

The model gave both figures, blended them into a rule that no longer applies, or picked the old one and sounded certain. In the third row the current page’s passage never reached the model at all: the archived copy took its slot. A stale duplicate doesn’t just add a wrong figure; it can crowd out the right one.

Better search can’t fix this, because search is working: both versions really are relevant. Which one is current is a fact about the documents, not in them.

Cause 2: the passage that never arrived

23 of the 106 wrong answers, from 8 questions. The right document was there; the paragraph or table row holding the answer wasn’t.

The clearest case asks: what probation period applies to a nine-month fixed-term contract? The policy has a table with the answer, four months. That row never reached the model on any setup, even with ten passages. What did arrive was a sentence saying probation for short contracts “will be outlined in their contract”. Every setup but one answered with that, confidently and with a citation; the current-documents setup refused.

I expected the re-ranker to rescue passages like this. It mostly couldn’t. On the answerability-gate setup, 19 answerable questions were missing part of their answer passage. I checked where each one ranked:

Eleven were shortlisted but ranked just below the six-passage cut. Eight never made the shortlist, so the re-ranker never saw them. Many of the hardest are table rows: “Up to 9 months → 4 months” shares almost no words with the question and means little on its own. What beat them was usually a sibling from the same document, or the near-duplicate archived copy from Cause 1.

Causes 3 to 5: the smaller ones

The first is the one cause that truly happens during generation: a summary that stops one sentence too early. In HR, legal or medical text, that sentence is often the exception that applies to the reader.

The second is a safety net doing harm. A checker whose only move is deletion will cut sentences that merge two sources or are mostly right. Flagging or rewriting would do less damage.

The third matters beyond my numbers. If an AI grader judges your answer quality, part of what you’re chasing may be the grader. Read a sample of failures before you fix anything.

What fixed what

I tested the two fixes aimed at the two biggest causes, each added on top of the answerability-gate setup.

Dropping superseded documents worked. A six-line record lists each superseded document and what replaced it. Passages from a superseded document are dropped before the six are chosen, so a current passage takes the slot. Of the 12 questions behind Cause 1, 8 are now answered correctly and 2 are refused rather than guessed. Across all 132 questions it got 10 right that the gate setup got wrong, and 3 the other way round. With this sample that is suggestive rather than proof, but it was the largest gain in the project, and it came from six lines of metadata.

Showing ten passages was a mixed result. The answer passage now arrived 87% of the time instead of 78%, and it answered more questions. But accuracy fell back to 84%: it fixed 8 answers and broke 8 others. The longer context invited longer answers that wandered into the extra material, such as adoption rules added to a paternity answer. Getting the passage in is necessary, not sufficient.

Diagnosing your own system

If your retriever finds the right documents and the answers are still poor, check these in order:

  1. Write down the evidence, not just the document. For 50 to 100 test questions, copy the exact sentence or table row the answer needs.
  2. Measure passage recall next to document recall. A large gap between them is your first suspect.
  3. Split your failures in two. Evidence never arrived: a retrieval and chunking problem. Evidence arrived: a generation problem. They need different fixes.
  4. Look for old versions. Check how often a superseded passage lands in the context. Mine did on almost half the questions.
  5. Check your tables. A row cut away from its column headings is nearly impossible to retrieve and easy to misread.
  6. See what fills the slots. When the right passage misses the cut, look at what beat it.
  7. Diff drafts against final answers. If anything edits answers after generation, compare its input and output on your failures.
  8. Read the failures yourself before trusting the grader. Some of them won’t be failures.

What this doesn’t show

  • It’s small. 106 wrong answers from 34 distinct questions. Many are the same question failing on several setups, so the percentages lean towards the questions that failed most often.
  • It’s one library. HR policies and statutory-pay pages are dense with numbers, conditions and yearly updates. A library without old versions would put more weight on the other causes.
  • It’s one generator. Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite wrote every answer. In the first article, Claude was more careful about conflicting sources but still repeated planted figures, so a stronger model moves these numbers without removing the causes.
  • The labels are one reader’s. They were written with AI assistance: each wrong answer got one main cause, assigned by reading it against the reference and the passages shown, and I have not had them checked independently. They are in the repository to check and argue with.

The code, the evidence passages and every labelled answer are on GitHub: github.com/sandeshjung/rag-safety-ladder. You can also browse every setup’s answers online, side by side with the passages each one was shown.

Sources

The documents

  • HR policies: Kettering General Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, policies and procedures
  • GOV.UK: Maternity pay and leave, Paternity pay and leave, Shared Parental Leave and Pay, Statutory Sick Pay, National Insurance rates and allowances. The archived 2025 versions are earlier copies of the same pages. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

The models

  • Answers: Google Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite
  • Claim checking and grading: OpenAI gpt-oss-120b on Groq
  • Search: BAAI bge-small-en-v1.5, BM25 and the ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 re-ranker

This project

  • Code, evidence passages and labelled answers: github.com/sandeshjung/rag-safety-ladder
  • Results viewer: rag-safety-ladder on Streamlit

title: I Tested 10 Ways to Stop an AI Chatbot From Lying. The Fix Wasn’t the AI.
excerpt: Better search, citations, fact-checking and confidence thresholds left accuracy flat. Telling it which documents were genuine and current took it from 77% to 93%.
content:
Better search, citations, fact-checking and confidence thresholds left accuracy flat. Telling it which documents were genuine and current took it from 77% to 93%.

The problem: a wrong answer that sounds right

You ask your company’s HR chatbot how much annual leave you get. It answers instantly, politely and with a citation. It’s wrong. You book the holiday anyway.

An AI that says “I don’t know” is mildly annoying. An AI that confidently gets your pay, your leave or your rights wrong can cost you real money. So I built an assistant with three rules:

  1. Answer only from the documents. No guessing from general knowledge.
  2. Show your sources. Every claim points to the page it came from.
  3. Say “I don’t know” when the documents don’t say.

Then I measured how often it actually kept them. The measuring turned out to be the interesting part.

What I built: a ladder, not a single system

The library was 33 real documents: HR policies from a UK hospital trust plus official GOV.UK pages on statutory pay. The assistant works like most company chatbots. It searches the documents for relevant passages, then asks an AI model to answer from those passages only. This is called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG.

Rather than build the “best” version straight away, I built a ladder. Each rung adds one feature to the rung below, so each one’s effect can be measured on its own. Rungs A to F are the standard safety playbook. G to J are fixes I added after seeing what A to F got wrong.

Two AI models do the work, both on free tiers:

My expectation was simple: every rung up should make it a little more honest. The data disagreed.

How I tested it: questions designed to catch it out

I wrote 256 test questions. Half are straightforward; the rest are traps.

For the last group I asked Claude to write 25 fake documents and slipped them into the library. They look like ordinary HR memos, each with a figure that contradicts the real policy and a hidden instruction aimed at the AI. Anyone who can save a file to a shared drive can do the same.

Every rung answered the same 132-question sample (same mix of types) and all 25 fake-document questions. A separate AI graded each answer against a reference answer I wrote, and I checked that grader against my own judgement (more on that below).

Running this on free tiers takes a lot of time. About 22 hours of actual computing, some 5,000 AI calls, took eight days of calendar time, most of it waiting for daily limits to reset. I tried to upgrade to Groq’s paid developer tier to speed it up, but it wasn’t available: sign-ups were paused due to high demand.

Finding 1: the standard upgrades didn’t make it more accurate

Better search, re-ranking, citations, a sentence-by-sentence checker and a confidence threshold: six rungs of textbook RAG safety. Accuracy bounced between 73% and 82%, in no steady direction, and every rung sits inside every other rung’s margin of error.

The upgrades did change how much it answered, from 58% to 66% of questions. They didn’t change how often it answered questions it should have refused: 10% at rung A, 13% at rung F, both with a margin of about ±7 points.

So the upgrades bought more answers, not more honesty. The next three findings explain why.

Finding 2: its confidence score barely knew when it was wrong

Rung F refuses when its confidence is low. I built that confidence from three common-sense signals: consistency (ask three times, do the answers agree?), backing (how many sentences did the checker confirm?) and search strength (how clearly did the best passage stand out?).

On ordinary questions the combined score tracked correctness only weakly (+0.20, where 0 is chance and 1 is perfect). With fake documents in the library it turned the wrong way (−0.22). A fake written to match a question stands out in search, so the system grew more confident exactly when it was being fooled.

A refusal rule is only as good as the confidence behind it. “The AI was consistent” and “the AI checked itself” are not evidence that it was right.

Finding 3: fake documents didn’t hijack it, they fooled it

The usual worry about planted documents is prompt injection: hidden text that takes control of the AI. Across 250 runs (25 fakes, ten rungs), I found no case of the AI obeying a hidden instruction.

Then I checked whether the answers were right. They weren’t.

The AI wasn’t taking orders from the fakes. It was believing them. A memo that looks like a policy supplement gets treated as one, and the assistant reports what it says, citation and all. At rung D, 15 of 25 answers cited a fake.

The sentence checker couldn’t help. It confirmed 15 of the 18 claims that cited a fake, and it was right to: the fake really did say that. A checker that asks “does the source say this?” can’t ask “should I trust this source?”

Would a smarter model fix it?

I gave Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 exactly the same 25 prompts, fakes included.

Claude was far better at noticing that something was off, but it still couldn’t tell which document was genuine. Most of its answers laid out the real figure and the fake one side by side and told the reader to check with HR. A smarter model turns silent capture into a visible conflict. It doesn’t close the hole, because which document to trust is information about the documents, not in them.

Finding 4: it found the right document and still got it wrong

When a chatbot answers wrongly, the usual suspect is search. Not here: in 123 of the 124 wrong answers across every rung, the correct document was among the passages the AI was shown.

So I went through the 106 wrong answers from rungs A to G one by one and labelled why each went wrong, with AI assistance.

The biggest cause was old and new versions of the same thing. Real libraries are full of them: a superseded policy nobody deleted, last year’s statutory pay rates beside this year’s. Faced with two figures, the AI gave both, blended them or picked the old one. “You can get £116.75 per week or up to £123.25 per week” is cited, polite and useless.

Only 2 of the 106 were the AI reasoning badly from good evidence. Most of the damage was done before it wrote a word, by what the documents said and which passages reached it. That gap is the subject of a [Your RAG Found the Right Document. So Why Is the Answer Still Wrong?](https://medium.com/@sandeshjung/your-rag-found-the-right-document-so-why-is-the-answer-still-wrong-a3b304cedff1).

Finding 5: knowing which documents to trust, and which are current, is what worked

The findings point at three gaps: the system can’t tell when it doesn’t know, can’t tell a real document from a fake, and can’t tell an old version from the current one. I added one rung for each, then one more.

G · Answerability gate. Before writing anything, a second AI looks at the passages and asks: do these actually contain the answer? If not, it refuses. It checks the evidence rather than the answer, so a confidently wrong answer can’t talk its way past it. It stopped 29 of the 36 questions the documents couldn’t answer, and accuracy rose from 77% to 85%.

H · Provenance register. Only documents on an approved list, with a fingerprint of their contents, can reach the AI. Not one fake got through, and accuracy with fakes present doubled, from 35% to 71%. The caveat is built in: my fakes were never registered. The risk moves to whoever controls the list. (A cheaper rule, “trust anything with a reference number and approval date”, blocked every fake but also rejected 16 of 23 real policies and all 10 GOV.UK pages.)

I · Prefer current documents. A six-line record of which document replaced which. Passages from a replaced document are dropped before the AI sees them. This was the biggest gain of the project: accuracy went from 85% to 93%. Question by question it got 10 right that the gate got wrong, and 3 the other way round.

J · Ten passages instead of six. The answer passage often ranked just below the top six, so I showed it ten. The answer passage arrived more often, but answers wandered into the extra material and accuracy fell back to 84%. More context isn’t free.

With 132 questions each rung’s accuracy carries a margin of about ±7 points, and the fake-document figures (25 questions) about ±15. The gains from G and I are the strongest signals in the data, but they are evidence, not proof.

Checking my own homework

Two of my own mistakes nearly made it into this article.

My scorecard punished the right answer. Early results said citations made the assistant answer more questions it should have refused. Reading them one by one, six were false-premise questions where it correctly said “that’s not true, here’s what the policy says”. My scorecard counted any answer to those as a failure. Once fixed, the “upgrades make it worse” story disappeared.

A bug made the confidence finding look worse than it was. The code that read citations was silently dropping every citation to a GOV.UK page, so the checker saw only about half the claims. After fixing it and re-running everything affected, the confidence score turned out to be weakly right on normal questions and wrong only under attack. A smaller headline, and a truer one.

I also checked the AI grader against my own judgement on 42 answers:

Its mistakes ran both ways, so it isn’t quietly flattering the system. But 42 answers is a small sample, and I reviewed pre-drafted labels rather than labelling blind. Every number in an AI evaluation is only as good as the scorecard behind it.

What I’d tell anyone building one

  • Measure before you add safety features. Most of mine sounded right and measured as neutral.
  • Test with trick questions. An assistant that aces normal questions can still invent answers its documents never cover.
  • Don’t trust the AI’s confidence in itself. Check any confidence signal against graded answers before it makes decisions.
  • Control who can add documents, and keep a list of what’s genuine. The real threat was a believable fake memo, not a clever hidden command.
  • Clean up old versions. Telling my system which version was current lifted accuracy from 85% to 93%, more than any other change.
  • Read the actual answers. One of my headline findings was wrong because of my own scorecard.

Citations make an AI answer look trustworthy. Looking trustworthy and being right are measured separately, and only one of them is easy to fake.

Try it yourself

The code, the 256 questions and every recorded answer are on GitHub: github.com/sandeshjung/rag-safety-ladder. You can also explore the results online: pick any test question and read what each rung answered side by side, with the passages it was shown, which ones it cited, and whether any were fakes or out of date. No sign-up needed. With your own free Gemini and Groq keys, you can ask it your own questions live; the keys are used for that request only and never stored.

Sources

The documents

  • HR policies: Kettering General Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, policies and procedures
  • GOV.UK: Maternity pay and leave, Paternity pay and leave, Shared Parental Leave and Pay, Statutory Sick Pay, National Insurance rates and allowances. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.
  • The 25 planted documents are fictional, written for this experiment.

The models

  • Answers: Google Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (free-tier limits)
  • Checking and grading: OpenAI gpt-oss-120b, served by Groq
  • Search: BAAI bge-small-en-v1.5 and the ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 re-ranker
  • Comparison: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5

  • Code, questions and every recorded answer: github.com/sandeshjung/rag-safety-ladder
  • Results viewer: rag-safety-ladder on Streamlit

title: We Costed an AI Audit System Two Ways. The Fine-Tuned Model Won, But Not for the Reason Everyone Says.
excerpt: A real cost breakdown for building document-heavy AI systems in the UK and Europe, with September 2026 prices.
content:
A real cost breakdown for building document-heavy AI systems in the UK and Europe, with September 2026 prices.

It is a incredibly common question in engineering leadership right now.

“Should we fine-tune our own model, or just call the API?”

The question is almost always triggered by a company’s first massive OpenAI or Anthropic bill — and the mild panic that follows. Naturally, teams expect the answer to be, “Fine-tune it, it’s cheaper.” But while that is sometimes right, it’s usually for much narrower reasons than people think. For many teams, it’s flatly wrong.

So instead of arguing about it in the abstract, I costed a real system both ways.

First, a thing that changed and nobody told you

Before the numbers, one piece of housekeeping that quietly reshaped this whole debate.

You cannot fine-tune a current frontier model.

OpenAI’s own pricing page now says it is winding down the fine-tuning platform. It is closed to new users, and the only model still listed for tuning is o4-mini at $100 per training hour. Anthropic has never offered fine-tuning through its own API. The one path that ever existed was Claude 3 Haiku supervised fine-tuning on Amazon Bedrock, and Haiku 3 is now retired outside Bedrock and Google Cloud.

So when someone says “fine-tune versus frontier” in late 2026, what they actually mean is:

Take an open-weight model — Qwen, Llama, a Nemotron, gpt-oss — train a LoRA adapter on your data, and serve it yourself or through a host like Fireworks or Together.

That is a different decision with a different risk profile. Worth being precise about it before you put it in a board deck.

The system we costed

Not a toy. A full audit-evidence platform for a mid-size firm, the kind of thing a UK or Nordic accounting practice actually buys.

Here is what it does, end to end:

  1. Intake. Documents land from the client portal. Invoices, purchase orders, goods-received notes, bank statements, lease contracts, board minutes. Mostly scanned PDFs.
  2. Classification. Each document gets a type and gets routed to the right test.
  3. Extraction. Pull structured fields into a fixed schema. Vendor, date, net, VAT, PO reference, approver, currency, cost centre. Output must be valid JSON that matches the schema exactly, every time.
  4. Control testing. Three-way match. Does the invoice agree with the PO and the goods-received note? Is the approver inside the delegated authority limit? Most of this is plain code, not a model.
  5. Exception triage. Anything that fails a test gets scored and ranked.
  6. Workpaper drafting. The system writes the first draft of the finding. “We tested 42 payments above the £50,000 threshold. Three lacked documented secondary approval.”
  7. Auditor Q&A. The auditor asks questions across the whole engagement file and gets grounded answers with citations back to source documents.

Steps 2 and 3 are where almost all the tokens go. They are also the most boring, most repetitive, most schema-bound parts of the system. Steps 6 and 7 are where the judgement lives, and they are a rounding error on volume.

That split is the entire story. Hold onto it.

Where the tokens go

For costing, assume documents are OCR’d to text before a model sees them. That avoids vision-token pricing and it is what you would do anyway.

Per document, across three calls (classify, extract, self-check):

  • ~5,200 input tokens — the document, the schema, a few worked examples
  • ~600 output tokens — the JSON

Two volumes:

  • Pilot: 100,000 documents a month. One firm, one busy season.
  • Scale: 2,000,000 documents a month. The same product sold to fifty firms.

That works out to 580 million tokens a month at pilot, and 11.6 billion at scale.

The numbers

List prices, standard tier, global routing, no batch or cache discounts. All verified against the vendors’ own pricing pages in September 2026.

At pilot volume, the whole argument collapses. Running the entire extraction pipeline on Claude Sonnet 5 costs $1,640 a month. On Haiku 4.5, $820. The fine-tuned 8B model costs $116.

You will not recover the cost of building a fine-tune by saving $1,500 a month. Not even close. Ship on the API.

At scale volume, it starts to look like a real decision:

  • Claude Opus 5: $82,000/month
  • GPT-5.6 Sol: $65,600/month
  • Claude Sonnet 5: $32,800/month
  • Claude Haiku 4.5: $16,400/month
  • GPT-5.6 Luna: $3,520/month
  • Fine-tuned 8B, serverless: $2,320/month

The headline everybody wants to write is “fine-tuning saved 93%.” That number is real, and it compares the fine-tune to Opus 5. But you should never have been running bulk invoice extraction on Opus 5. Comparing your optimised architecture against someone else’s worst architecture is not analysis, it is marketing.

The uncomfortable finding

Look at the bottom two rows again.

GPT-5.6 Luna: $3,520. Fine-tuned 8B: $2,320.

The gap is $1,200 a month. Fourteen thousand dollars a year.

Building that fine-tune properly means labelling data, writing an eval harness, running training, standing up serving, and wiring monitoring for drift. Call it eight engineer-weeks. Whatever your blended European contract rate is, multiply it out. At most rates I have seen, you are looking at somewhere north of eighteen months to pay that back on token savings alone.

So here is the honest version:

The biggest single cost win is not fine-tuning. It is routing.

Moving classification and extraction off the flagship and onto the cheapest competent tier takes Opus-5 economics down from $82,000 to $3,520 a month. That is a 96% reduction, and you can do it in an afternoon with a router and a decent eval set. The fine-tune, on top of that, buys you another 34%.

The training cost, for what it’s worth, is almost free. Fireworks charges $0.50 per million training tokens for LoRA supervised fine-tuning on models up to 16B. Twenty thousand labelled examples at 2,500 tokens each, three epochs, is 150 million training tokens. Seventy-five dollars a run. Eight runs during development is $600.

The GPU time was never the expensive part. The data and the evaluation are. Anyone quoting you a fine-tuning project based on compute cost has not built one.

So why fine-tune at all?

Two reasons. Neither is the token bill.

Reason one: schema adherence

This is the part that matters for audit specifically, and it is badly under-discussed.

A frontier model is a generalist. Ask it to return one of 51 fixed subcategories and it will occasionally invent a 52nd, because inventing plausible things is what it was trained to do. In a chatbot that is a minor annoyance. In a workpaper that feeds a signed audit opinion, it is a defect.

There is a 2026 preprint on security document classification that measured exactly this. On a benchmark with a fixed 51-subcategory taxonomy and a strict JSON output protocol, a fine-tuned local model beat prompted frontier models by 15–20 percentage points. The authors observed GPT-5 inventing subcategory names that did not exist in the taxonomy. Their explanation is the interesting part: on loosely-formatted extraction tasks, frontier models do fine. Under strict schema constraints, calibration beats reasoning.

Another preprint found a fine-tuned Qwen2.5–0.5B — half a billion parameters, runs on a single consumer GPU — scoring 0.83 average micro-F1 on general-domain relation extraction against 0.69 for GPT-5.4 and 0.66 for Claude Sonnet 4.6 under a minimal zero-shot protocol. The authors are careful to say this does not make small models intrinsically stronger. It shows that targeted task adaptation is worth more than raw capability on a narrow, fixed task. That is exactly what audit extraction is.

Anthropic published a similar result from their own fine-tuning work on Claude 3 Haiku: classification accuracy went from 81.5% to 99.6% on a comment-moderation task, with 85% fewer tokens per query. Different domain, same shape of finding.

For an audit product, a two-point accuracy gain on field extraction is worth more than the entire inference bill. Every miss becomes a human review. Human review is the expensive thing in this business.

Reason two: you know where the data is

This is the one that decides deals in Europe.

The EU residency problem

If your client is a UK or EU accounting firm, their audit files contain client financial data, employee data, and sometimes personal data belonging to third parties. “Where does this run” is not a nice-to-have question. It is the second thing procurement asks.

Here is the current state of play, and it surprises people:

Anthropic’s first-party API does not offer EU data residency. The inference_geo parameter accepts global or us. US-only costs 1.1x. There is no EU option. If you need Claude inside the EU, you route through AWS Bedrock or Google Vertex in an EU region, and regional endpoints carry a 10% premium over global. Claude on Microsoft Foundry still has no EU data zone as of writing.

OpenAI does offer regional processing, at a 10% uplift for models released on or after 5 March 2026.

Fireworks charges a 1.5x premium for region-restricted dedicated deployments.

Your own GPUs in a Frankfurt or Dublin data centre cost whatever they cost, and the answer to “where does the data go” is “nowhere.”

Run the scale-volume numbers again with residency priced in:

Two dedicated H100s running your fine-tuned 8B model, region-restricted, twenty-four hours a day, comes to about $17,520 a month. Claude Sonnet 5 through a Bedrock EU endpoint at the same volume is $36,080. Opus 5 is $90,200.

That is the real EU case for owning your model. Not that it is cheaper per token. That the compliance story is a sentence instead of a diagram.

But don’t buy GPUs too early

The flat-rate GPU line is seductive and it traps people. It only wins above a volume most products never reach.

Against two dedicated H100s at global pricing ($11,680/month):

  • Claude Sonnet 5 stays cheaper below ~700,000 documents a month
  • Claude Haiku 4.5 stays cheaper below ~1.4 million
  • GPT-5.6 Luna stays cheaper below ~6.6 million

Most audit products will spend their first two years to the left of all three of those lines. Serverless hosting of your own fine-tuned model sidesteps the problem entirely — you get the custom weights without the idle GPU bill — which is why it is where I would start every time.

The decision framework

Strip out the noise and it comes down to four questions.

1. What is your monthly token volume, honestly? Below roughly a billion tokens a month, use the cheapest competent frontier tier and move on. You have better places to spend eight engineer-weeks. Fine-tuning at pilot volume is engineering theatre.

2. Is the task narrow and schema-bound? Fixed output format, fixed label set, thousands of near-identical examples a day. That is a fine-tune. Open-ended reasoning, judgement calls, drafting a narrative for a partner to sign — that is a frontier model, and it always will be.

3. Where does the data have to live? If a contract clause says “processing must remain in the EEA,” that changes the shortlist before cost enters the conversation. Price the residency premium at the start, not after the architecture review.

4. Do you have 10,000 labelled examples, or a way to get them? NVIDIA Research’s position paper on small models in agentic systems puts the rule of thumb at 10,000 to 100,000 examples for fine-tuning a small model. If you do not have that, your first project is not a fine-tune. It is instrumenting your frontier-model pipeline so it logs its own training data.

That last point deserves emphasis, because it is the pattern I recommend most often and it is the one nobody markets.

Ship on the frontier API. Log every call. Six months later you have a labelled dataset that cost you nothing, and you fine-tune from a position of knowledge instead of a position of hope.

The same paper estimates how much of three real open-source agent systems could move to small models: about 60% of LLM calls in MetaGPT, 40% in Open Operator, 70% in Cradle. Not 100%. Not zero. The answer is a mix, and you cannot guess which calls without the logs.

One counter-argument, stated fairly

Menlo Ventures’ enterprise survey found open-source models falling to 11% of enterprise workloads, down from 19%. While everyone was writing about how small models are the future, enterprises were consolidating onto closed frontier APIs. Anthropic took 40% of enterprise LLM spend, OpenAI 27%, Google 21%.

That is not a contradiction of everything above. It is a measurement of where the friction is. Closed APIs win on convenience, and convenience usually wins. The teams getting real value from open-weight fine-tunes are the ones who deliberately took on operational burden for a reason they could articulate. If you cannot articulate the reason, the survey is telling you something.

On the regulation, briefly

A quick note since UK and EU readers will ask.

The EU’s Digital Omnibus on AI — Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 — was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July. It pushed high-risk obligations for standalone Annex III systems from 2 August 2026 out to 2 December 2027, and for AI embedded in regulated products under Annex I to 2 August 2028.

What did not move: the Article 50 transparency obligations, which applied from 2 August 2026 as originally scheduled. Article 50(2) marking for systems already on the market applies from 2 December 2026.

An audit-support tool with a human sign-off gate generally does not land in Annex III. But check your own use case rather than taking my word for it, because if any part of your system touches hiring decisions or creditworthiness, it does. And none of this touches GDPR, which applies to the client data in your pipeline no matter how the AI Act classifies the system.

Demand for this is not theoretical, by the way. A Wolters Kluwer survey of 4,214 internal audit professionals found 39% already using AI and another 41% planning to adopt within twelve months.

What I’d actually tell a client

If you came to us with this build, here is the shape of the answer.

Phase one. Ship it on the cheapest frontier tier that passes your eval set. Instrument every model call. Get it in front of real auditors during a real busy season. Do not fine-tune anything.

Phase two. Read the logs. Find the two or three calls that account for most of your tokens. Check whether they are schema-bound and repetitive. They almost always are.

Phase three. Fine-tune those calls, and only those. Serve them serverless first. Keep the frontier model for triage, drafting and Q&A. Route between them.

Phase four. Move to dedicated GPUs only when volume or a residency clause forces it. Not before.

Four phases, and three of them are cheaper than the thing most people do on day one.

The question was never “small model or frontier model.” It was “which of my calls actually need to think.” Answer that and the cost question answers itself.

Sources

All figures verified September 2026. Prices change frequently — check them before you commit a budget.

  • OpenAI, API pricing and fine-tuning wind-down — developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing
  • Fireworks AI, serverless and training pricing — fireworks.ai/pricing and docs.fireworks.ai/serverless/pricing
  • Belcak et al., Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI, NVIDIA Research, arXiv:2506.02153
  • Security Document Classification with a Fine-Tuned Local Large Language Model, arXiv:2605.20368 (preprint)
  • Sub-Billion, Super-Frontier: Small Language Models Rival Zero-Shot Frontier LLMs, arXiv:2606.22606 (preprint)
  • Anthropic, Fine-tune Claude 3 Haiku in Amazon Bedrock — claude.com/blog/fine-tune-claude-3-haiku
