title: Stop Chasing the Best LLM — Find the Bottleneck Instead
excerpt: I have recently been seeing some version of the same question. Should I use GPT or Claude? Is Gemini better than DeepSeek? Which embedding model has the highest MTEB score? What’s the fastest…
content:
I have recently been seeing some version of the same question. Should I use GPT or Claude? Is Gemini better than DeepSeek? Which embedding model has the highest MTEB score? What’s the fastest inference provider?

These questions though repetitive are reasonable questions. However, they’re also, sometimes the wrong question to be asking first.

The assumption underneath such question is that a better application comes from choosing a better model. In practice, most AI systems don’t fail because a wrong LLM was used. They fail because someone optimized a part of the system that was not the actual bottleneck of the system.

A support chatbot giving bad answers usually doesn’t mean a smarter model is needed. Sometimes it might need a better retrieval. A coding assistant that feels slow usually doesn’t mean a fast inference provider is needed. Sometimes it might need fewer LLM calls in its loop. A RAG system hallucinating over your own documents usually doesn’t need another benchmark leader sitting behind it. It might need better embeddings or cleaner context reaching the model in the first place.

The job of an AI engineer isn’t choosing the smartest model anymore — benchmark websites and even LLMs themselves can help narrow that choice. The real job is identifying the weakest part of the system and improving it.

Every engineering hour spent optimizing the wrong component is an hour not spent improving the actual bottleneck. Spending days comparing GPT and Claude is wasted effort if your retriever is only finding the right document 60% of the time. Before optimizing anything, identify what’s actually limiting the system.

Every AI application is the same pipeline

Whether you’re building a chatbot, a coding assistant, a document search tool, or the agentic RAG loop, they’re all variations on the same shape: a user’s request goes in, something retrieves relevant context, that context gets assembled and checked, an LLM generated from it, and a response is provided. Every stage in that chain is a place the system can be quietly failing, and the LLM is only one of them.

You don’t upgrade the engine in a car when the tires are flat. In same way, LLM cannot be changed when retrieval is broken.

Bottleneck #1: The model

You should spend real time comparing models only after everything is ruled out. And even then, the first question isn’t “which model is best”. It’s “what’s the minimum model that clears my quality bar”. If a smaller, cheaper model answers 95% of your production queries correctly at a third of the cost and half the latency, that’s usually the better engineering decision, not a compromise.

Before you compare anything, eliminate hard constraints like budget per request (not per month — per request is what actually decides whether a design is viable at your volume), a p95 latency ceiling (the number 95% of your requests beat, which is what a user actually feels, not your average), a privacy or data-residency floor, and the context window you genuinely need. Then only you should start comparing reasoning quality, coding performance, or tool use.

One mention worthy mistake: picking a model because it advertises a million-token context window. Every frontier model claims one now, but advertised context and effective context are different numbers — current long-context benchmarks show multi-fact retrieval accuracy dropping 30 to 60 points once you’re past roughly 200k tokens, even on models that headline a 1M window. If your workload actually lives in that range, test it there specifically. Don’t take the spec sheet’s word for it.

In addition, public benchmarks alone cannot be trusted to make final call. They’re useful for narrowing a shortlist, not for picking a winner. Run 100 to 200 real examples from your own workload through your finalists and compare the actual outputs before you commit to anything.

Bottleneck #2: Retrieval

This is one of most underrated bottleneck. For many RAG applications, improving retrieval quality — through better embeddings, chunking, reranking, or indexing — often produces larger gains than switching to a stronger LLM. On a typical RAG workload, the embedding model alone can shift retrieval precision by 20 to 30%. If the wrong documents get retrieved in the first place, it doesn’t matter how capable the model downstream is. It can’t invent the right answer when a wrong context is provided.

What’s actually worth evaluating are: multilingual support if you need it, retrieval quality on benchmarks matched to your task, dimensionality, inference speed, storage cost, and price per token.

Dimensionality is the trade-off most teams get wrong by not thinking about it at all. Doubling embedding dimensions doesn’t double retrieval quality — for most applications, 768 to 1024 dimensions is close to practical ceiling for what you gain, while going from 1536 to 3072 dimensions costs roughly 6x the storage for a marginal quality improvement. If your vector database is holding millions of documents, that’s not a rounding error.

The other thing worth knowing before selecting: swapping LLMs might take you few minutes. Whereas, swapping embedding models means rebuilding your entire vector index from scratch, which might take hours or even days depending upon the corpus size. Choose this one more carefully than you’d choose the model, not less — it’s the harder decision to undo.

One area that’s often overemphasized is prompt engineering. A better prompt can absolutely improve outputs, but its impact is bounded by the information reaching the model. If retrieval returns the wrong documents or incomplete context, no amount of prompt tweaking will consistently recover the right answer. Prompt engineering should refine a good system, not compensate for a broken one.

Bottleneck #3: Orchestration

Most people assume latency comes from slow models. However, many times it comes from too many model calls.

Taking a simple agentic RAG loop that: decomposes the question, retrieves, validates what came back, reformulates and retries if it wasn’t good enough, then finally generates. That will already have five LLM calls for a single user question, before you ever added a router, a reranker, or a second validation pass. Swapping in a model that’s 30% faster barely moves the needle if the loop itself is making five calls it didn’t need to make.

The highest-leverage fixes here usually aren’t model changes at all: prompt and context caching (skipping this specifically is one of the most common unforced errors — it can add on the order of 80% in avoidable cost), routing simple requests to smaller model instead of running everything through the frontier one, parallelizing retrieval calls that don’t actually depend on each other instead of looping through them sequentially, and cutting validation loops that aren’t earning their keep.

A fast system isn’t the one running the fastest model. It’s the one doing the least unnecessary work.

Bottleneck #4: Agent design

One of the more persistent misconceptions between the AI community is that more agents make a better system. Usually what they make is a more expensive and harder to debug. Every additional agent adds more prompts, more coordination, more latency, more tokens, and more places for the whole thing to fail quietly.

Production benchmarks put independent multi-agent setups at roughly 58% extra token overhead compared to a well-tuned single agent doing the same task, and centralized orchestrator topologies at closer to 285% extra for something a single agent handles just as well. Teams that start with 3 to 5 agents and scale only when the data supports it consistently outperform teams that launch with 10 or more.

One of the good practice would be to start with one well-scoped agent. Add a second only when there’s a specific, earned reason: the work genuinely decomposes into parallel sub-tasks, different sub-tasks need different tools or models, or two parts of the workflow need different permission boundaries — an agent that drafts a refund and a separate one that’s actually allowed to issue it is a legitimate split. “It felt like it should be multi-agent” is not a specific, earned reason.

Bottleneck #5: Infrastructure

Eventually you do have to pick a provider — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, Fireworks, self-hosted, or some mix. By this point the model itself is often the smaller part of the decision. What actually matters more: rate limits, regional availability, SDK maturity, the pricing structure (cached input pricing and batch discounts can move your real cost more than the headline per-token price), observability, and uptime.

The decision framework

Whenever you’re tempted to ask “which LLM should I use,” ask this instead: what’s actually limiting this system right now?

If the answers are wrong, inspect retrieval. If they’re slow, inspect orchestration. If costs are high, inspect routing. If retrieval itself is poor, inspect embeddings. Only once those check out should you spend time comparing models — and even then, on your own workload, not a public leaderboard.

AI engineering has changed

A few years ago, success in AI meant building better models. Today, it means building better systems. Tomorrow, the best AI engineers won’t be defined by the models they use, but by their ability to diagnose, optimize, and ship reliable AI applications.

Sources

  • Long-context retrieval accuracy at 200K+ tokens, via ofox.ai’s 2026 Long-Context LLM Benchmarks
  • Embedding model selection criteria, MTEB rankings, and dimensionality/cost trade-offs, via Ailog’s 2026 Embedding Models Benchmark and Tensoria’s 8 Embedding Models Compared for Production RAG
  • Multi-agent token overhead and production deployment sizing, via Decode the Future’s 2026 Multi-Agent Systems Explained and DEV Community’s Multi-Agent Systems guide
  • LLM selection framework (hard constraints, benchmark-then-verify methodology), via LLMTest’s 2026 definitive guide to choosing an LLM and Zoopa’s Practical Guide to Choosing the Right LLM

title: Iron Man’s Jarvis Is Almost Ready — And It Explains the Evolution of AI
excerpt: When I first started my AI journey, shaving half a point off the error rate on MNIST was a legitimate research event. Many people built careers on incremental gains against benchmarks most outsiders…
content:
When I first started my AI journey, shaving half a point off the error rate on MNIST was a legitimate research event. Many people built careers on incremental gains against benchmarks most outsiders had never heard of. Today, the dominant way to “do AI” is to open an API key, wire an existing model into a business workflow, and ship. Same field. Almost an unrecognizable profession.

What practicing AI used to require

The way (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b² is drilled into every algebra student, y = mx + b was drilled into every AI practitioner. Linear regression is the first thing anyone learns in this field. For a long time, a huge amount of real work never went much further than variations on it — fit a line, fit a curve, fit a decision boundary. Even now, financial services, healthcare, supply chain, retail, and energy still rely heavily on linear regression.

Neural networks changed what was possible, but they came with a price: backpropagation. I remember doing math for days before writing a single line of training code — deriving the chain rule by hand across every layer, working through why a particular gradient update was stable before trusting it enough to actually run. Only after that did the coding start, and even then you were building the model itself: reading research papers, choosing an architecture, engineering features by hand, tuning a training loop that might run for days to weeks before you knew if it worked.

Understanding backpropagation properly took me the better part of a week — chasing down papers, working through derivations, piecing together a real understanding from sources that were never written to teach a beginner. Today you can open a chatbot, ask it to walk you through backpropagation step by step, and have a working derivation in front of you in minutes. It’s not just that the work got easier. The barrier to learning the work nearly disappeared too.

Progress was measured in benchmarks. MNIST, then ImageNet, then whatever came next. A fractional accuracy improvement was worth publishing. That was the job: build a model, one problem at a time, from something close to first principles.

Math didn’t disappear. It got compiled away.

Here’s the part I think is actually the throughline of the whole story, not just a nostalgic detail: every layer of progress in this field has worked the same way. Something that used to require deep, hard-won expertise gets absorbed into a tool, and the next generation of practitioners doesn’t have to relearn it from scratch.

Hand-derived gradients became autodiff — PyTorch and TensorFlow started doing the calculus for you. Hand-built architectures became pretrained models — transfer learning did the design for you. Pretrained models became foundation model APIs — a single API call did the training for you. And now, foundation models are becoming agentic systems — a framework does the orchestration plumbing for you.

Nobody derives gradients by hand anymore, yet understanding them remains invaluable when training becomes unstable or a model behaves unexpectedly. Infrastructure replaced the repetition, not the understanding.

The abstraction didn’t just change how we build AI — it changed how we learn it. That’s a strange kind of recursion: the tool built from decades of hard-won expertise is now the fastest way to acquire that expertise in the first place. Each step didn’t make the field shallower. It moved the floor up and freed practitioners to work one layer higher than before. That’s the strange beauty of building something powerful enough: it eventually makes the struggle to build it unnecessary for the next person.

Two breakthroughs that changed everything

Two pieces of research stand out for changing the course of AI. The first is XGBoost. When it showed up in 2014, gradient-boosted trees weren’t new, but XGBoost was fast and effective. It became dominant for years — it was hard to find a winning Kaggle solution on structured, tabular data that didn’t use it. For a huge share of real business problems, XGBoost was about as state-of-the-art as it got. Like autodiff, it turned years of optimization research into a single library call — proof that strong engineering and an optimized implementation could outperform a more complex idea, not just a bigger one. It was the workhorse of an entire era of practical machine learning. Even today, many production systems use it.

The second is the one that actually broke the field open: “Attention Is All You Need,” published in 2017. Before it, sequence models were built on recurrence — architectures like RNNs and LSTMs that processed one step at a time. These structures made training slow and hard to parallelize. The Transformer architecture that paper introduced replaced recurrence with self-attention — letting a model weigh every part of a sequence against every other part at once, in parallel.

That single architectural change is the reason large language models exist at the scale they do. Parallelizable training meant you could throw enormously more compute and data at a model than a recurrent architecture could ever practically absorb. XGBoost proved you could win without deep learning. Attention Is All You Need proved you could go bigger with it than anyone had realistically planned for.

All of these findings are the reasons we’re where we are now: foundation models became good enough that the interesting work moved from building them to orchestrating them.

The unit of work changed

The shift can be summarized in one sentence: it moved from training to orchestrating. Almost nobody is training a new classifier from scratch to route support tickets anymore. They’re taking an existing LLM and shaping its behavior with prompts, retrieval, and tool access — deciding what it can see, what it can do, and when it should ask for more information instead of guessing.

That’s the entire premise behind agentic RAG, which I’ve been writing about in this series: you’re not training anything. You’re building a loop around a model that already exists — deciding when it should retrieve more context, when it should validate what it found, when it should try again. The skill moved from model-building to system-building.

The warning underneath the opportunity

Here’s where I think people get this wrong: they see “prompt engineering” and “agentic building” exploding in demand and assume that’s the skill to chase. I’d be careful. It reminds me of the years when everyone wanted to study IT because the demand was high — until the demand caught up with the supply, and just knowing how to use a computer stopped being a differentiator at all.

If history repeats itself, building agentic applications is likely heading toward the same fate. It’s valuable right now — for many people, “doing AI” simply means developing agentic applications. But I don’t think that advantage will last. Frameworks are already absorbing more of the orchestration work, just as autodiff absorbed the calculus. The skill that feels essential today is only one abstraction layer away from becoming a platform feature.

The fundamentals didn’t vanish. They’re what separates someone who can debug a broken system from someone who can only assemble one when the framework’s defaults stop working. I believe agentic-building skill is about to split the same way. The engineers who only know how to wire a framework together will be exposed the moment the framework gets good enough to do it for them. The engineers who understand what’s happening underneath will be the ones who can move to whatever the next layer turns out to be. This is where I believe companies hiring for such engineers should focus.

The brain

Whenever I think about where all this is heading, I end up thinking about Iron Man’s Jarvis — not as a metaphor, but as an actual technical comparison. I used to always wonder how magical Jarvis felt. Maybe what made Jarvis feel like science fiction when I was growing up wasn’t that he could talk — it was how he could reason, plan across steps, use tools, understand context, and correct himself when he got something wrong.

In many ways, we already have that. LLMs can do most of what made Jarvis feel impossible — the core reasoning capability is basically here. I saw a post saying Iron Man is just someone with unlimited Claude tokens — with what we’re getting to experience, I wouldn’t deny that. What’s missing now is a body: natural voice instead of typed text, persistent memory instead of a fresh context window every time.

That’s why “agentic” is the right word for this exact moment in the field. It’s not a new kind of intelligence but an assembly. Which is also why the voice AI numbers happening right now aren’t really a side story — they’re the last major component of Jarvis getting built in real time.

Big tech is racing on this too — multilingual voice, personalized assistants tuned to each user — and the money backs up the urgency. Voice AI funding surged roughly eightfold in a single year, reaching around $2.1 billion in 2025. Nearly 80% of the world’s top 50 banks are already running production voice agents, up from about a third of them just two years ago. And almost a quarter of Y Combinator’s latest cohort is building voice-first rather than text-first products.

Text in, text out was never the endpoint. It was simply the interface that happened to be easiest to ship first. The gap between “chatbot” and “Jarvis” was never really about reasoning capability anymore — it’s the interaction layer, and that’s exactly where the industry’s attention is moving now.

Where that leaves you

If you’re building a career in this field right now, I’d take two things from this. First: the market is real, and applied, system-building AI skills are genuinely in demand — that part isn’t hype. Second: don’t mistake “in demand today” for “durable.” The specific skill of wiring an existing model into a workflow is going to keep getting easier and more automated, the same way training a model got easier and more automated before it.

The practitioners who’ll still matter once that happens aren’t the ones who only learned to assemble agentic applications. They’re the ones who paired that skill with an actual understanding of the fundamentals underneath it — the same fundamentals I spent days grinding through math for, years ago, before I ever got to write a line of training code. That foundation is what lets you move to whatever the next layer turns out to be, instead of getting stranded when this one gets automated too.

Looking back, shaving half a point off MNIST wasn’t really the point. If history keeps repeating, the systems we’re painstakingly wiring together today will eventually become someone else’s API call.

Jarvis was a fictional character when I was growing up. Watching this field move as fast as it has, that fiction feels closer than it’s ever been — not because the brain got smarter overnight, but because we’re finally building everything around the brain.

Sources

  • Chen, T. & Guestrin, C., “XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System” (2016)
  • Vaswani, A. et al., “Attention Is All You Need” (2017)
  • Voice AI funding, deployment, and market-size figures, via Ringly’s 47 Voice AI Statistics for 2026

title: Building an Agentic RAG System from Scratch
excerpt: By the end of this article, you’ll have implemented an agentic RAG system twice: once from scratch to understand every moving part, and once with LlamaIndex and LangGraph to see how production…
content:
By the end of this article, you’ll have implemented an agentic RAG system twice: once from scratch to understand every moving part, and once with LlamaIndex and LangGraph to see how production frameworks encapsulate the same logic.

Everything here runs on Gemini’s free API tier through Google AI Studio, so you can follow along without a credit card. You can also use Groq’s API instead — I’ll show the swap where it matters.

What we’re building

We’re going to build a small Q&A agent over a fictional API product’s documentation — call it “ByteFlow API.” (A chatbot suggested the name when I asked it to draft some sample product documentation.) Five short docs: pricing, rate limits, error codes, authentication, and webhooks. Small enough to read in under a minute, but structured so that some questions genuinely need more than one doc at once — which is exactly what demonstrates an agentic workflow.

That last part matters most. If every test question is answerable from a single doc, traditional RAG looks just as good as agentic RAG. So our test question is deliberately multi-hop:

“I’m on the free plan and I got blocked after a bunch of requests today. What’s happening and what are my options?”

Answering that well means combining the rate-limits doc (what a block actually is), the pricing doc (what “free plan” means for limits), and the errors doc (what to actually do about it). One vector lookup against one doc won’t cover all three.

Setup

Grab a free API key from Google AI Studio, then:

pip install google-genai torch
import os
os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"] = "your-key-here"  # or use a .env file

We’ll use gemini-embedding-001 for embeddings and gemini-3.6-flash for generation. Google renames and reshuffles Gemini model versions fairly often, so check the current list in AI Studio and swap in whatever's current — nothing else in this code depends on the specific model name.

Using Groq instead?

pip install groq
import os
os.environ["GROQ_API_KEY"] = "your-key-here"  # or use a .env file

I like llama-3.3-70b-versatile for generation on Groq. Model and embedding selection for different providers is worth its own article — this one sticks to Gemini as the default, with the Groq swap shown where the generation code lives below.

Part 1 — Building the loop by hand

No framework yet. The point of this section is to make the agent loop boring and mechanical — because that’s exactly what it is once you strip the framework abstraction away.

The document set and a simple vector index

We don’t need a real vector database for five documents — a plain Python list and cosine similarity is enough. This is a demo of agentic RAG, not a vector database benchmark.

One design detail matters more than it looks like it should: the answer to our test question can’t live entirely inside one document. The three facts a complete answer needs — why you got blocked, what the actual tier numbers are, and what your options are — are deliberately split across rate_limits, pricing, and errors, with no single doc containing enough to answer alone. If they overlapped, a single embedding lookup could accidentally grab the one doc that covers everything, and the whole point of the comparison would disappear.

import os
import json
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from google import genai
from google.genai import types

client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"])
GEN_MODEL = "gemini-3.6-flash"
EMBED_MODEL = "gemini-embedding-001"
DOCS = [
    {
        "id": "pricing",
        "text": (
            "ByteFlow API pricing tiers: Free tier costs $0 per month and includes "
            "100 requests per day, with no webhook access. Pro tier costs $29 per "
            "month and includes 10,000 requests per day, plus webhook access. "
            "Enterprise tier has custom volume pricing and is billed annually."
        ),
    },
    {
        "id": "rate_limits",
        "text": (
            "Rate limits are enforced per API key, not per account, and reset "
            "daily at midnight UTC. Exceeding your allotted requests for the day "
            "returns an HTTP 429 response for the remainder of the current window. "
            "Your specific daily request cap depends on your subscription tier - "
            "see the pricing page for exact tier-by-tier numbers."
        ),
    },
    {
        "id": "errors",
        "text": (
            "Error code reference: 401 means an invalid or missing API key. 429 "
            "means you have exceeded your rate limit for the current window. 500 "
            "means an internal server error, and requests should be retried with "
            "backoff. If you're seeing repeated 429 responses, you can wait for "
            "your daily window to reset, or move to a higher-volume subscription tier."
        ),
    },
    {
        "id": "auth",
        "text": (
            "To authenticate requests, pass your API key in the Authorization header as "
            "a Bearer token, e.g. 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY'. Keys are generated "
            "from the dashboard under Settings > API Keys."
        ),
    },
    {
        "id": "webhooks",
        "text": (
            "Webhooks let you receive real-time events when data changes, instead of "
            "polling the API. Webhook access is only available on Pro tier and above. "
            "Configure your endpoint URL from the dashboard under Settings > Webhooks."
        ),
    },
]

def embed_text(text, task_type="RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT"):
    result = client.models.embed_content(
        model=EMBED_MODEL,
        contents=text,
        config=types.EmbedContentConfig(task_type=task_type),
    )
    return torch.tensor(result.embeddings[0].values)

def build_index(docs):
    for doc in docs:
        doc["embedding"] = embed_text(doc["text"], task_type="RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT")
    return docs

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return F.cosine_similarity(a.unsqueeze(0), b.unsqueeze(0)).item()

def retrieve(query, docs, top_k=2):
    query_emb = embed_text(query, task_type="RETRIEVAL_QUERY")
    scored = [(doc, cosine_similarity(query_emb, doc["embedding"])) for doc in docs]
    scored.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)
    return [doc for doc, score in scored[:top_k]]

def generate(prompt):
    response = client.models.generate_content(model=GEN_MODEL, contents=prompt)
    return response.text

Using Groq for generation instead? Swap in this version of generate (embeddings still go through Gemini, since Groq doesn't serve an embedding model):

from groq import Groq
groq_client = Groq(api_key=os.environ["GROQ_API_KEY"])
GEN_MODEL = "llama-3.3-70b-versatile"

def generate(prompt):
    response = groq_client.chat.completions.create(
        model=GEN_MODEL,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=0.2,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Nothing agentic yet — this is just the standard plumbing every RAG system needs.

The traditional baseline

Here’s the traditional RAG baseline we’re improving on:

def traditional_rag(query, docs):
    chunks = retrieve(query, docs, top_k=2)
    context = "

".join(chunk["text"] for chunk in chunks)
    prompt = (
        f"Answer the question using only the context below.

"
        f"Context:
{context}

Question: {query}"
    )
    return generate(prompt)

Embed, retrieve, generate. One shot, no questions asked about whether what came back was actually good enough.

Adding the agent loop

This is the actual point of this article. Four pieces, in order.

1. Decompose. Embedding models produce a single vector representing the entire sentence. If one sentence contains multiple intents, that vector averages them together. Splitting the query lets each embedding focus on one semantic objective, improving retrieval precision.

def decompose(query):
    prompt = (
        "Break the following question into 1-3 self-contained sub-questions "
        "needed to answer it fully. Respond with a JSON array of strings, "
        "nothing else.

"
        f"Question: {query}"
    )
    raw = generate(prompt)
    cleaned = raw.strip().strip("`").replace("json", "", 1).strip()
    try:
        return json.loads(cleaned)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return [query]

The try/except here matters more than it looks like it should. Even when explicitly asked for JSON only, LLMs will occasionally wrap the response in a code fence or add a stray sentence — without this fallback, that kind of formatting hiccup would crash the whole run on what looks like a perfectly reasonable prompt.

2. Validate. For each retrieved chunk, ask whether it actually helps answer the sub-question it was retrieved for:

def grade_relevance(sub_query, chunk_text):
    prompt = (
        f"Question: {sub_query}

Passage: {chunk_text}

"
        "Does this passage help answer the question? Reply with only YES or NO."
    )
    verdict = generate(prompt).strip().upper()
    return verdict.startswith("YES")

We’re using a simple binary relevance grader here for clarity. Production systems often use numeric relevance scores or cross-encoder rerankers instead.

3. Reformulate. If nothing came back relevant, rewrite the query instead of giving up:

def reformulate(sub_query):
    prompt = (
        f"This search query returned nothing useful: '{sub_query}'. "
        "Rewrite it as a broader or differently-worded query that might "
        "retrieve better results. Reply with only the rewritten query."
    )
    return generate(prompt).strip()

4. The orchestrator. This is what ties decompose → retrieve → validate → retry → generate into an actual loop. It also prints a trace of what it did at each step — for a system with this many moving pieces, “what actually happened” is worth seeing, not just trusting:

def agentic_rag(query, docs, max_retries=2, verbose=True):
    sub_queries = decompose(query)
    evidence = []
    for i, sub_query in enumerate(sub_queries, start=1):
        if verbose:
            print(f"Sub-query {i}:")
        attempt = 0
        current_query = sub_query
        found = False
        while attempt <= max_retries and not found:
            chunks = retrieve(current_query, docs, top_k=2)
            if verbose:
                print("Retrieve ->")
                for chunk in chunks:
                    print(chunk["id"])
            relevant_chunks = [
                chunk for chunk in chunks if grade_relevance(sub_query, chunk["text"])
            ]
            if verbose:
                print("Validated:")
                for chunk in relevant_chunks:
                    print(f"✓ {chunk['id']}")
            if relevant_chunks:
                evidence.extend(relevant_chunks)
                found = True
            else:
                current_query = reformulate(current_query)
                attempt += 1
    if not evidence:
        return "I couldn't find enough reliable information to answer that."
    seen_ids = set()
    unique_evidence = []
    for chunk in evidence:
        if chunk["id"] not in seen_ids:
            unique_evidence.append(chunk)
            seen_ids.add(chunk["id"])
    if verbose:
        print("Final evidence:")
        for chunk in unique_evidence:
            print(chunk["id"])
    context = "

".join(chunk["text"] for chunk in unique_evidence)
    prompt = (
        f"Answer the question using only the context below. If the context "
        f"includes conflicting information, point out the conflict.

"
        f"Context:
{context}

Question: {query}"
    )
    return generate(prompt)

Run it against the test question below and you’ll get output shaped like this:

Sub-query 1:
Retrieve ->
rate_limits
errors
Validated:
✓ rate_limits
Sub-query 2:
Retrieve ->
pricing
auth
Validated:
✓ pricing
Final evidence:
rate_limits
pricing

Notice errors shows up under Retrieve -> but never gets a ✓ — it was fetched but didn't pass grade_relevance, so it's correctly absent from Final evidence. That's the trace doing its job: it shows the difference between what was fetched and what was actually used, which is exactly the gap a system with no validation step can't show you at all, because it never checks.

Notice what’s not here: no framework, no special “agent” class, no magic. It’s a loop with an escape hatch (max_retries), a print statement at each step, and a dedup step, calling the same four functions above in sequence. That's genuinely most of what "agentic RAG" means at the implementation level — everything else is refinement on top of this shape.

Running both side by side

if __name__ == "__main__":
    indexed_docs = build_index(DOCS)  
    test_question = (
        "I'm on the free plan and I got blocked after a bunch of requests "
        "today. What's happening and what are my options?"
    )
    print("--- Traditional RAG ---")
    print(traditional_rag(test_question, indexed_docs))
    print("
--- Agentic RAG ---")
    print(agentic_rag(test_question, indexed_docs))

Run it yourself and compare the two outputs. The agentic_rag call will print its trace first, then the answer underneath it. What you should see: the traditional version embeds the whole question as one vector, which lands closest to rate_limits and errors — both are directly about being blocked — and its answer explains the 429 and tells you to wait or upgrade, but without the actual numbers, since pricing never gets pulled in. The agentic version decomposes the question, and one of its sub-queries ends up closer to something like "what tier limits and upgrade options are available," which retrieves pricing specifically — so its final answer includes the concrete numbers (100/day free, 10,000/day Pro) that the traditional version left out.

If you run this yourself and the two answers still come out equally complete, that’s worth noticing rather than ignoring — it usually means the embedding model found enough signal in rate_limits and errors combined to imply the tier structure even without the pricing doc, or that decompose didn't produce a sub-query specific enough to isolate pricing. Both are realistic failure modes, not bugs in the code — and they're exactly the kind of thing context-recall evaluation (covered in a later article in this series) is built to catch systematically instead of by eyeballing one run.

Part 2 — Rebuilding it with LlamaIndex and LangGraph

Same demo, same docs, same test question. This time, LlamaIndex handles indexing and retrieval, and LangGraph handles the loop as an actual state machine instead of a hand-rolled while loop.

pip install llama-index llama-index-llms-google-genai llama-index-embeddings-google-genai langgraph nest-asyncio

A heads-up if you’re running this in Jupyter: LlamaIndex’s GoogleGenAI integration calls asyncio.run() internally on every complete() call. Jupyter already runs its own event loop in the background, and Python won't let you nest a second asyncio.run() inside one that's already running. So without a fix, the decompose node will fail with RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop the moment you invoke the graph.

import nest_asyncio
nest_asyncio.apply()

Indexing — what LlamaIndex replaces

Compare this to the embed_text / build_index / cosine_similarity / retrieve block from Part 1:

import os
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, Document, Settings
from llama_index.embeddings.google_genai import GoogleGenAIEmbedding
from llama_index.llms.google_genai import GoogleGenAI
API_KEY = os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"]
Settings.embed_model = GoogleGenAIEmbedding(model_name="gemini-embedding-001", api_key=API_KEY)
Settings.llm = GoogleGenAI(model="gemini-3.6-flash", api_key=API_KEY)
DOCS = [
    "ByteFlow API pricing tiers: Free tier costs $0 per month and includes 100 "
    "requests per day, with no webhook access. Pro tier costs $29 per month and "
    "includes 10,000 requests per day, plus webhook access. Enterprise tier has "
    "custom volume pricing and is billed annually.",
    "Rate limits are enforced per API key, not per account, and reset daily at "
    "midnight UTC. Exceeding your allotted requests for the day returns an HTTP "
    "429 response for the remainder of the current window. Your specific daily "
    "request cap depends on your subscription tier - see the pricing page for "
    "exact tier-by-tier numbers.",
    "Error code reference: 401 means an invalid or missing API key. 429 means "
    "you have exceeded your rate limit for the current window. 500 means an "
    "internal server error, and requests should be retried with backoff. If "
    "you're seeing repeated 429 responses, you can wait for your daily window "
    "to reset, or move to a higher-volume subscription tier.",
    "To authenticate requests, pass your API key in the Authorization header as "
    "a Bearer token, e.g. 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY'. Keys are "
    "generated from the dashboard under Settings > API Keys.",
    "Webhooks let you receive real-time events when data changes, instead of "
    "polling the API. Webhook access is only available on Pro tier and above. "
    "Configure your endpoint URL from the dashboard under Settings > Webhooks.",
]
documents = [Document(text=t) for t in DOCS]
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)
retriever = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=2)

The VectorStoreIndex handles all chunking, embedding, and cosine-similarity search — the same steps Part 1 built by hand.

The loop as a state graph

This is where LangGraph earns its keep. Instead of a while loop with a manual retry counter, the loop becomes an explicit graph with nodes and conditional edges:

import json
from typing import TypedDict, List
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    query: str
    sub_queries: List[str]
    evidence: List[str]
    retries: int
    sufficient: bool
    answer: str

def decompose_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    prompt = (
        "Break the following question into 1-3 self-contained sub-questions. "
        "Respond with a JSON array of strings, nothing else.

"
        f"Question: {state['query']}"
    )
    raw = Settings.llm.complete(prompt).text
    cleaned = raw.strip().strip("`").replace("json", "", 1).strip()
    try:
        sub_queries = json.loads(cleaned)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        sub_queries = [state["query"]]
    return {**state, "sub_queries": sub_queries, "evidence": [], "retries": 0, "sufficient": False}

def retrieve_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    new_evidence = list(state["evidence"])
    for sub_query in state["sub_queries"]:
        nodes = retriever.retrieve(sub_query)
        new_evidence.extend(node.text for node in nodes)
    return {**state, "evidence": new_evidence}

def validate_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    prompt = (
        f"Question: {state['query']}

Evidence:
"
        f"{chr(10).join(state['evidence'])}

"
        "Is this evidence enough to answer the question fully? Reply with only YES or NO."
    )
    verdict = Settings.llm.complete(prompt).text.strip().upper()
    sufficient = verdict.startswith("YES")
    return {**state, "sufficient": sufficient, "retries": state["retries"] + (0 if sufficient else 1)}

def reformulate_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    prompt = (
        f"This search didn't return enough to answer: '{state['query']}'. "
        "Rewrite it as a broader or differently-worded question that might "
        "retrieve better results. Reply with only the rewritten question."
    )
    reformulated = Settings.llm.complete(prompt).text.strip()
    return {**state, "query": reformulated, "sub_queries": [reformulated]}

def route_after_validate(state: AgentState) -> str:
    if state["sufficient"] or state["retries"] > 2:
        return "generate"
    return "reformulate"

def generate_node(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    context = "

".join(dict.fromkeys(state["evidence"]))
    prompt = (
        f"Answer using only this context, and flag any conflicts:

"
        f"{context}

Question: {state['query']}"
    )
    return {**state, "answer": Settings.llm.complete(prompt).text}

graph = StateGraph(AgentState)
graph.add_node("decompose", decompose_node)
graph.add_node("retrieve", retrieve_node)
graph.add_node("validate", validate_node)
graph.add_node("reformulate", reformulate_node)
graph.add_node("generate", generate_node)
graph.set_entry_point("decompose")
graph.add_edge("decompose", "retrieve")
graph.add_edge("retrieve", "validate")
graph.add_conditional_edges(
    "validate", route_after_validate, {"reformulate": "reformulate", "generate": "generate"}
)
graph.add_edge("reformulate", "retrieve")
graph.add_edge("generate", END)
app = graph.compile()

Five nodes now, matching Part 1’s five pieces one for one: decompose, retrieve, validate, reformulate, generate. validate records a sufficient flag directly rather than making route_after_validate infer success from the retry count — that distinction matters: without a separate flag, a second attempt that succeeds would leave retries at 1, which is indistinguishable from "still failing," and the graph would loop forever instead of moving on. When validate finds the evidence insufficient, it routes to reformulate — which rewrites the query, exactly like Part 1's reformulate function — and reformulate loops back to retrieve. That loop repeats up to twice before route_after_validate gives up and moves on to generate anyway, same cap as Part 1's max_retries=2.

Notice that the control flow is now described declaratively. Instead of Python deciding what happens next line by line, the graph defines the possible transitions up front — which is what makes retries, branching, and checkpointing much easier to manage as the graph grows.

result = app.invoke({
    "query": "I'm on the free plan and I got blocked after a bunch of requests today. What's happening and what are my options?",
    "sub_queries": [], "evidence": [], "retries": 0, "sufficient": False, "answer": "",
})
print(result["answer"])

Line count is actually a bit longer than Part 1’s version here — LangGraph’s overhead only starts paying off once the graph gets more complex than four nodes, or once you need the things it gives you for free: automatic state persistence between steps, the ability to checkpoint and resume a run that failed halfway through, and a graph structure you could visualize.

Visualize your graph

from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(app.get_graph().draw_mermaid_png()))

Tradeoffs

  • Visibility. In Part 1, every retry, every validation call, every prompt is a plain function you can print, breakpoint, or step through. In Part 2, a decent amount of that lives inside VectorStoreIndex and Settings.llm.complete — still inspectable, but one layer further away.
  • Boilerplate. LlamaIndex cut the retrieval code by more than half — a real win the moment you go from 5 documents to 5,000, where you’d otherwise be hand-rolling chunking strategies and batched embedding calls.
  • State handling. LangGraph’s AgentState and conditional edges are more code up front for a 4-node graph, but they stop being "more code" the moment you need to persist state across a crash, add a fifth node, or run this as part of a larger multi-agent system.

Real production agentic RAG systems layer in more — reranking, hybrid retrieval, tool routing, structured outputs, observability, caching, guardrails — but all of it builds on the same loop you just implemented twice: decompose, retrieve, validate, retry, generate. Everything else is refinement on top of that shape.

title: Agentic RAG vs. RAG: Why Your Retrieval Pipeline Needs to Start Reasoning

content:
Agentic RAG Systems

A support agent asks your AI assistant why their invoice changed this month. Your RAG pipeline embeds the question, pulls back a generic help article about how billing works, and confidently tells the customer nothing useful — because the actual answer was sitting in a SQL table it never queried. This is the failure mode that’s quietly pushing every serious RAG system toward something more agentic: retrieval that reasons about what it’s missing instead of retrieving once and hoping.

What is RAG?

2023 RAG, or traditional RAG, is a technique where an AI model retrieves information from a knowledge base and generates its response. The AI queries a knowledge base, retrieves information, and then generates a response.

The pipeline is a straight line, and the diagram above shows exactly how short it is: encode your documents and index them in a vector database — commonly Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, or just pgvector inside an existing Postgres instance — encode the incoming query the same way, run a similarity search to pull back the most similar documents, and hand that retrieved context — plus the original query — to the LLM as a single prompt. Seven steps, one pass, done. There’s no step in that flow where the system stops to ask “was that actually the right context?”

That’s the gap agentic RAG was built to close.

What is agentic RAG?

Modern RAG, or agentic RAG, is more dynamic. The AI agent actively manages how it gets information, integrating RAG into a reasoning loop. It’s no longer just retrieving — it’s constantly refining its queries using reasoning. It’s a more intelligent system now. The system decides whether to retrieve, what to retrieve, how many times to retrieve, and when to stop — the same way a person would re-search Google after skimming the first result and realizing it needs more evidence to answer the question.

You can see that reasoning play out in the diagram above. The agent doesn’t just embed and search — it rewrites the initial query, asks itself “do I need more details?”, decides which source will actually help (vector database, tools/API, or the open internet), retrieves, and then — critically — asks a second question before it ever shows the user anything: “is the answer relevant?” If the answer is no, it loops back and tries again rather than shipping a weak response. That evaluate-and-retry cycle, steps 9 through 12 in the diagram, is the piece traditional RAG simply doesn’t have.

The practical trigger for going agentic is query complexity. If your queries are single-hop and unambiguous, a straight traditional retrieval pipeline is cheaper and just as accurate — agentic loops add latency and orchestration cost without a quality payoff. Agentic RAG is at its best when you have multi-hop questions, ambiguous intent, tasks that span multiple data sources, or workflows where the agent must also act.

Why do AI agents need access to dynamic knowledge?

To see why that loop matters, it helps to zoom out from RAG specifically and look at what AI agents are built to do in the first place — and why a fixed snapshot of information was never going to be enough for them.

AI agents are sophisticated AI systems designed to operate on their own. They’re “information robots” that “perceive, reason, plan, and act,” as NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has described them. These agents understand problems, make plans, use different tools, and understand different types of information — text, images, structured data.

An AI agent’s core capabilities break down into four pieces:

  • Perceiving / Query understanding — understanding their surroundings and the context of a situation.
  • Reasoning — breaking down complex problems and strategizing solutions.
  • Planning — creating a step-by-step path to a goal.
  • Acting — executing tasks by using different tools.

Every one of those four depends on information that’s actually current. A model’s training data is a snapshot — frozen at a point in time — but the things an agent gets asked about keep moving: prices change, tickets get resolved, policies get updated, inventory shifts by the hour. An agent that can only pull from a fixed, one-time retrieval has no way to perceive the current state of anything — it’s reasoning over a photograph while the world it’s describing has already moved on. That’s what “dynamic” knowledge means here: not just more data, but data the agent can go re-check at the moment it’s actually needed.

An agent that can only retrieve once, from one source, with no way to judge what came back, isn’t really doing any of that reasoning or planning either — it’s just running a lookup. Both problems point in the same direction: retrieval needs to be something the agent actively controls, not a single step it passes through once.

Why was agentic RAG needed?

Zoom back into retrieval specifically, and the traditional pipeline starts showing cracks against those expectations. There were several recurring issues with the traditional RAG system:

  • No query decomposition: Complex, multi-part questions get embedded as a single vector. The retriever returns a mishmash of loosely related chunks that don’t cleanly address any individual sub-question.
  • No validation: The pipeline can’t evaluate whether retrieved chunks are actually relevant. Irrelevant context gets passed directly to the LLM, which generates plausible but unsupported answers — contributing to hallucinations on anything multi-hop.
  • Single-source constraint: Standard pipelines connect to one knowledge base. If your answer requires data from a vector store, a SQL database, and a live API, you have to build that orchestration yourself.
  • No retry logic: If the first retrieval attempt misses, there’s no mechanism to reformulate and try again. You get one shot.

These are structural limitations, not edge cases — and they’re exactly why agentic RAG has caught on so fast.

How agentic RAG addresses those limitations

Agentic RAG systems replace that fixed pipeline with an agent-controlled loop. It cycles through planning, retrieval, evaluation, and refinement until it has enough evidence to generate an answer. Each of the four limitations above maps to a specific piece of that loop.

Query decomposition and source routing

Query decomposition replaces single-vector embedding. Instead of collapsing a multi-part question into one embedding and hoping the nearest neighbors happen to cover every part of it, the agent first reasons about the question’s structure. Each sub-query gets routed to the most appropriate source. Rather than being wired to one vector store, the agent treats retrieval itself as a decision: which source is likely to have this answer? Factual lookups go to structured databases. Semantic queries go to vector stores. Time-sensitive questions go to web search or live APIs.

This routing decision is itself an LLM call. The agent acts as a classifier, examining each sub-question and selecting from its available tools. In practice, you define these tools explicitly, and the agent’s instructions tell it when to use each one — this is exactly the pattern frameworks like LangGraph and LlamaIndex are built to orchestrate: LlamaIndex typically owns the retrieval side (indexing, chunking, source connectors), while LangGraph handles the routing and state management around it.

Multi-hop retrieval

Some questions require chaining multiple retrieval steps, where the output of one informs the input to the next. RAG agents handle this by maintaining a scratchpad of intermediate results. After each retrieval, the agent decides whether it has enough context or needs to retrieve more. Systems like RQ-RAG formalize this by decomposing multi-hop queries into ordered sub-questions. RAG-Fusion takes a parallel approach instead, generating multiple reformulations of the same query and merging results using reciprocal rank fusion to improve recall.

Self-correction and retrieval validation

In a traditional pipeline, whatever the retriever returns goes straight to the LLM. The model can’t tell good context from bad. Agentic RAG adds a validation step: the agent scores each retrieved chunk for relevance before deciding whether to include it, discard it, or re-query.

This self-correction is what really distinguishes agentic retrieval from the traditional pipeline. The agent treats retrieved data as evidence to evaluate, not ground truth. When chunks conflict, the agent can retrieve additional context to resolve the contradiction rather than passing the conflict straight to the LLM and hoping for the best.

Reflection and memory

Advanced agentic RAG systems add two mechanisms on top of the retrieval loop. Reflection lets the agent review its draft answer, identify gaps or weak support, and trigger additional retrieval if needed. Memory operates at two levels: short-term memory tracks what’s already been retrieved in the current session (avoiding redundant calls), while long-term memory stores patterns from past queries to improve future routing and decomposition.

Putting it together: a concrete example

Say a customer support agent gets asked: “Why did my invoice change this month, and is this a known billing bug?”

A traditional RAG pipeline embeds that whole sentence as one vector, searches a single knowledge base (probably a help-docs vector store), and generates an answer from whatever comes back — usually a generic article about how invoicing works, with no actual answer about this customer’s this invoice.

An agentic system handles it differently, step by step:

  1. Decomposition — the agent splits the question into two sub-queries: “what changed on this customer’s invoice this month?” and “is there a known billing bug matching this change?”
  2. Routing — the first sub-query goes to the billing SQL database (structured, factual). The second goes to the vector store holding engineering/support docs (semantic).
  3. Multi-hop chaining — the SQL result comes back showing a line-item price increase. That detail becomes part of the input to the second retrieval, so the doc search is now specifically about that line item, not billing in general.
  4. Validation — the agent checks the retrieved doc against the SQL result. If the doc says the bug was already patched two weeks ago, but the SQL data shows the change happened yesterday, the agent flags the contradiction and re-queries — checking the support ticket system for a possible recurrence — instead of confidently telling the customer it’s a known, already-fixed bug.

That’s the whole loop from the diagrams above, applied to one real question: decompose, route, chain, validate, and only then answer. A traditional pipeline can’t do any of steps 2 through 4 — it has one vector store and one shot.

Designing an agentic RAG system with reasoning

Once you’ve decided you need that loop, there are still several architectural choices to make. The right one depends on query complexity, data structure, and your latency budget.

Query planning and decomposition strategies

The simplest approach is prompt-based decomposition: the agent is instructed to break a complex query into sub-queries before retrieving. More sophisticated systems use a dedicated planning step, where the agent generates a full retrieval plan up front.

Plan-and-execute architectures separate the planner from the executor. The planner reasons through the full task and produces a step-by-step plan. The executor runs each step and returns results to the planner for evaluation. This separation cuts costs, because the executor can run on a smaller, faster model while the planner handles the heavier reasoning.

Graph RAG and structured knowledge sources

Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph from your documents and retrieves via graph traversal instead of similarity search. For domains where information is inherently relational, graph-based agentic retrieval consistently outperforms flat vector retrieval on complex reasoning tasks.

The tradeoff is that knowledge graphs are expensive to build and maintain. They work best for stable, high-value datasets, where the upfront investment in graph construction pays off over many queries.

Routing agents, ReAct agents, and plan-and-execute agents

Three agent patterns show up most often in agentic RAG systems:

  • Routing agents — a routing agent examines the query and selects the most appropriate retrieval tool or data source. It doesn’t plan multi-step workflows, it just picks a lane.
  • ReAct agents — ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) agents interleave thinking and tool use. The agent reasons about what to do, takes an action, evaluates the result, and reasons about the next step. This pattern handles open-ended queries well but can get expensive, since it makes multiple LLM calls per iteration.
  • Plan-and-execute agents — these separate planning from execution entirely. The planning agent produces a full workflow up front. The execution agent runs each step without calling back to the planner until it finishes or hits an error. Completion rates tend to be higher and costs lower, because the executor isn’t re-planning at every step.

You rarely build these primitives from scratch. LangGraph is the common choice when you need durable, stateful orchestration with checkpointing across long-running loops. CrewAI has the lowest barrier to entry for role-based, multi-agent setups if you’re prototyping a routing or plan-and-execute pattern quickly. AutoGen leans toward multi-agent conversational patterns, where a supervisor agent delegates to specialist agents and synthesizes their results. For graph-based retrieval specifically, Microsoft’s open-source GraphRAG is the reference implementation most teams start from.

Monitor, evaluate, and debug agentic RAG pipelines

All of that extra reasoning comes with an extra burden: agentic RAG systems introduce multiple points of failure that single-pass RAG simply doesn’t have. Retrieval accuracy alone accounts for roughly 60% of RAG quality variance — the rest comes down to how well the generator processes and uses the context it’s given. Evaluating only the retrieval step leaves major blind spots in system performance. A system can retrieve perfect context and still produce a wrong or fabricated answer — this is called the “accuracy fallacy,” where a pipeline looks healthy end-to-end while quietly hallucinating.

Every agent run involves multiple LLM calls, tool invocations, and retrieval steps. You need traces that capture the full chain: what query the agent decomposed, which tools it called, what each tool returned, how the agent evaluated relevance, and what it decided to do next. Without end-to-end traces, debugging a bad answer means guessing which step went wrong.

That means tracking metrics at every layer, not just the final output. Tools like Ragas, DeepEval, and TruLens ship prebuilt scorers for most of these out of the box, and platforms like LangSmith or Arize Phoenix handle the end-to-end tracing across LLM calls and tool invocations:

  • Context precision — are the retrieved chunks actually relevant to the query?
  • Context recall — were all the chunks needed for a complete answer retrieved? (This is where multi-hop questions quietly fail — the generator answers fluently from partial context while precision-only dashboards stay green.)
  • Faithfulness — is the generated answer supported by the retrieved context, with no fabricated claims?
  • Answer relevance — does the answer actually address what the user asked?
  • Hallucination — a reference-free safety net scored on the final output alone.

Guardrails for prompt injection and output validation are just as important. Agentic RAG systems are vulnerable to prompt injection because the agent incorporates retrieved text directly into its reasoning context — a malicious document sitting in your knowledge base could hijack the agent’s behavior. Output guardrails validate that generated answers stay within expected bounds: no leaked system prompts, no fabricated citations, no off-topic responses.

The other layer worth implementing is hybrid search validation — confirming that semantic search results and keyword-based retrieval return consistent, non-contradictory context before synthesis. When the two diverge significantly, that’s usually a signal to re-query rather than merge conflicting evidence.

Production tradeoffs and when not to use agentic RAG

None of this makes agentic RAG a strict upgrade over traditional RAG. The benefits and the engineering cost need to be weighed against each other.

Latency and cost overhead of iterative retrieval

Every iteration in the agent’s loop involves at least one LLM call and one retrieval call. A multi-hop query that requires three retrieval cycles costs roughly three times as much as single-pass retrieval, and takes proportionally longer.

Complexity of agent orchestration at scale

More agents mean more failure modes. RAG agents can select the wrong tool, enter infinite retry loops, or produce inconsistent results across runs. Multi-agent systems introduce coordination overhead on top of that: agents can compete for resources, deadlock on shared state, or produce conflicting intermediate results.

Feedback loops that surface retrieval failures back to the planner are essential here. Without them, a subtle ingestion error or a stale index goes undetected until a user surfaces a bad answer.

Choosing between simple RAG and agentic RAG

Put together, that’s a practical decision framework:

Traditional RAG isn’t a lesser version of agentic RAG — it’s the right tool when your questions are simple and your data lives in one place, and no amount of looping fixes a problem you don’t actually have. Agentic RAG earns its cost when the question itself demands it: multiple sources, multiple hops, or an answer that needs to be checked before it’s trusted. The real skill isn’t picking a side — it’s building the simple pipeline first, watching where it actually breaks on real user queries, and adding just enough of the loop to fix that specific gap. That’s a more durable approach than architecting for complexity you’re guessing you’ll need.

title: Functions in JavaScript
